L05 Frequency Response: , Sinusoidal Steady State and Pole-Zero Geometry

Why this matters in the exam: Frequency response is the second half of Lecture 5 (“Frequency domain characteristics of LTI systems”, slides 27–35). It has never been examined. Sample Test 1 (20 marks, 50 min) stops at Weeks 1–4: sampling, signal operations, system properties, LCCDE and convolution. So there is no past-paper evidence of how many marks it gets. It is still core: Tutorial 4 Q3–Q7 are built on it, and L09 and T8 (notch filters, “rejects the frequency component completely”) assume you can do it. A multi-part question worth roughly 4–8 marks is likely: find , evaluate it at one or two frequencies, write the output, and sketch from a pole-zero plot.

1. The core ideas

1.1 Definition and the eigenfunction property (slides 27–29)

is the DTFT of the impulse response. It is periodic with period , so you only ever need . For real you only need , because and .

  • Trap: the input phase is kept and is added to it. The frequency never changes. A input stays a .

1.2 Convolution property: why the output can’t contain new frequencies

Wherever , too. An LTI system cannot create frequencies that are not in the input (slide 29). If an output has a frequency the input didn’t have, the system is nonlinear and/or time-varying (T4 Q5). The converse is false. A system that creates no new frequency for one test input can still be non-LTI. For example maps to itself, but it is time-varying.

The same property gives you from any input-output pair: (T4 Q3a).

1.3 from the LCCDE (slide 30)

Method: DTFT both sides. Every delay becomes (time-shift property). Then divide.

  • Trap 1: the course writes the with a minus sign on the right-hand side. If the equation is given as , then and the denominator is . Move all terms to the left and read the signs off directly.
  • Trap 2: this only gives the frequency response of a stable system (the slide says “of a stable LTI system”). That means all poles are inside the unit circle. If a pole sits on or outside the circle, “steady-state response” has no meaning.

1.5 Pole-zero (geometric) form (slides 31–34)

Multiply top and bottom by powers of :

Every factor is a vector from the zero to the point on the unit circle. With and :

Feature on the pole-zero plot Effect on as you walk round the circle
Zero on the unit circle at angle exactly (a null, used for notch filters)
Zero near the circle Deep dip near
Pole near the circle at angle Sharp peak near . The closer to the circle, the taller and narrower the peak.
Pole or zero at the origin No effect on (distance is always 1). Adds only linear phase .
Zero at / (blocks DC) / (blocks )
  • Trap: the vectors go from the pole or zero to . Measure the angle of that vector from the positive real axis. Getting the direction backwards adds to every angle.
  • Trap: the term. Count and the way the plot shows them. T4 Q7 has a double zero at the origin and two poles, and the course solution treats them as “” with no finite non-zero zeros. Either way gives the same answer, as long as you are consistent. A pole or zero at the origin contributes the angle itself, which is exactly the linear term.

2. The method

Recognise the question type.

Wording Playbook
“Determine the frequency response”, given an LCCDE or A
“Response to ”, “steady-state output” B
“The following input-output pairs have been observed… determine ” C
“Determine the frequency content… conclude whether LTI” D
“Sketch roughly the magnitude/phase” from a pole-zero plot, or “evaluate geometrically” E

Playbook A: find

  1. From : write . For an FIR filter it is just the taps times delays. For with use .
  2. From the LCCDE: put all terms on the left. Replace and . Then .
  3. For polar form: factor out the middle delay (symmetric FIR), or write (IIR).
  4. Sanity checks: and .

Playbook B: steady-state output to a sum of sinusoids

  1. List every input component with its frequency , amplitude and phase . A constant is . is . Keep as .
  2. Evaluate for each component as a complex number, then convert to and . Use exact values (, not 1.047) until the end.
  3. Write each output term as .
  4. Drop any term with and say so (“blocked by the zero at ”).
  5. Add the terms (superposition is allowed because the system is linear). DC terms: , and is real.
  6. For an IIR system, say it is the steady-state response: the stable poles’ transients have died out.

Playbook C: identify from input-output data

  1. If the input is a single complex exponential or sinusoid at , you get only . State that at other frequencies cannot be found (T4 Q3b).
  2. If the input is a general signal (exponential, finite sequence): using DTFT pairs.
  3. If the input is (check whether something like is really ), then the output is . DTFT it.
  4. With several sinusoid pairs and a known filter form (for example ), set up one equation per frequency and solve for the coefficients.

Playbook D: spot non-LTI systems

  1. Substitute into the system equation.
  2. Use trig identities: , , and .
  3. Reduce every frequency into . Use , so .
  4. If any output frequency is not in the input, the system is not LTI. Name the cause: a squared, product or constant term means nonlinear; a time-dependent coefficient or time-scaling means time-varying.
  5. If no new frequency appears, you cannot conclude it is LTI from this test alone.

Playbook E: geometric evaluation and sketching

  1. Mark the poles (×) and zeros (○). Ignore those at the origin for magnitude.
  2. Walk from (the point ) anticlockwise to (the point ).
  3. Check the key points: , , and the angle of every pole and zero near the circle. At each point estimate .
  4. Draw the sketch: zero on the circle means touching 0; pole near the circle means a peak, sharper the closer it is. Between features, draw a smooth curve.
  5. For a value, compute each vector length exactly with . Multiply by .
  6. For phase, add the angles of the zero vectors, subtract the angles of the pole vectors, and add . Watch for the jump when passes through a zero on the circle.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Dropping the input phase. The output of is . Both phases appear.
  • A negative “magnitude”. at is . The magnitude is and the phase gains , giving in T4 Q4. Writing an amplitude of with phase is equivalent, but a “magnitude response” sketch must be .
  • Wrong signs on the . Read the denominator from the equation with all terms on the left: .
  • Forgetting the DC and terms. A constant is a sinusoid at and is multiplied by . Using for DC is wrong unless . is .
  • Claiming from one sinusoid pair. One pair gives one value only (T4 Q3b).
  • “No new frequencies, so it is LTI”. That doesn’t follow. The test only proves non-LTI. and (which only adds DC) are both non-LTI.
  • Counting origin poles/zeros in . They have unit distance to the circle and don’t affect magnitude. They do affect phase through .
  • Reversing the vectors. Use (from the zero to the circle point), not . Reversing them adds per factor.
  • Leaving frequencies above . Reduce them: for a real cosine (T4 Q5c).

T4 Q6 (tutorial). Sketch roughly the magnitude of Fourier transforms, , corresponding to the pole-zero patterns given below.

Solution

Pole and zero positions below are estimated from the plots. Numbers in brackets come from evaluating those estimated patterns in Python. They are a guide to the shape, not official values.

The course solution says: walk round the unit circle. goes small near a zero and large near a pole. Poles or zeros at the origin have no effect on magnitude. Sketch .

(a) Double pole at the origin. Zeros on (or very near) the unit circle at . This is a second-order FIR notch, like . Shape: it starts at a moderate value at (about 0.59) and falls to zero at . It then rises steadily and smoothly to its maximum at (about 3.41), where is furthest from both zeros. It looks like a “V” notch near followed by a long rising curve.

(b) Double zero at the origin. Complex-conjugate poles inside the circle at about . Shape: a moderate value at , rising to a single rounded peak at , then decaying smoothly to a small value at . A resonance or band-pass shape. It does not reach zero anywhere, because there are no zeros on the circle.

(c) Eight zeros equally spaced on the unit circle at angles (, including and ). An 8th-order pole at the origin. This is , so . Shape: zero at , with four equal humps in between. The humps peak at , each with height 2. It is a comb filter.

(d) Zeros on the circle at . Poles at about . This is like . Shape: zero at , rising slowly and then steeply to a tall sharp peak at (about 10.5 for poles at radius 0.9), then falling back to zero at . It is symmetric about . A narrow band-pass shape, the same kind of curve as Figure 1 but centred at .

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

FREQUENCY RESPONSE (L05 slides 27-35)
H(w) = sum_n h(n) e^{-jwn}        H(0)=sum h(n)    H(pi)=sum (-1)^n h(n)
LCCDE (all y on left): H(w) = sum_k b_k e^{-jkw} / (1 + sum_k a_k e^{-jkw})
  stable system only (poles inside |z|=1)
e^{jwn}  -> H(w) e^{jwn}
A cos(wn+phi) -> A|H(w)| cos(wn + phi + theta(w))     (sin stays sin)
Sum of sinusoids: do each frequency separately, add. DC: w=0. (-1)^n: w=pi.
Y(w)=H(w)X(w): LTI never creates new frequencies.
  New freq appears -> NOT LTI (nonlinear and/or time-varying).
  No new freq -> proves nothing.
One sinusoid pair gives H at that ONE frequency only.  delta(n) in -> h(n) out.
Symmetric FIR: factor out middle delay: 1+e^{-j2Lw} = 2e^{-jLw}cos(Lw)
  |H| = |real part|; negative real part -> add pi to phase.
1/(1-a e^{-jw}): |H| = 1/sqrt(1-2a cos w + a^2)
GEOMETRY: H = b0 e^{jw(N-M)} prod(e^{jw}-z_k)/prod(e^{jw}-p_k)
  |H| = |b0| prod V_k / prod U_k   (lengths: zero->e^{jw}, pole->e^{jw})
  theta = angle b0 + w(N-M) + sum angle(e^{jw}-z_k) - sum angle(e^{jw}-p_k)
  zero ON circle -> |H|=0 there; pole near circle -> sharp peak
  origin poles/zeros: no effect on |H|, only linear phase
  zero at z=1 kills DC; zero at z=-1 kills w=pi
SKETCH: walk e^{jw} from z=1 (w=0) to z=-1 (w=pi); check 0, pi, pole/zero angles.
